Efficacy and safety of herbal stimulants and sedatives in sleep disorders

Charlotte Gyllenhaal1,3, Sharon L. Merritt2, Sara Davia Peterson1, Keith I. Block1,3 and Tom Gochenour3,4

1Program for Collaborative Research in the Pharmaceutical Sciences, College of Pharmacy, University of Illinois at Chicago, 833 South Wood Street, Chicago IL 60612,

2Center for Nacolepsy Research, College of Nursing, University of Illinois at Chicago, 845 South Damen Avenue, Chicago IL 60612, 3Institute for Integrative Cancer Care, 1800 Sherman, Suite 515, Evanston IL 60201 and 4College of Pharmacy,

University of Illinois at Chicago, Chicago IL 60612, USA

World-wide use of herbal medicines is increasing, following regulatory and manufacturing developments. Herbs are attractive alternative medications to many patients with sleep disorders, who may be averse to using conventional drugs. We review here the most common herbal stimulants and sedatives. Caffeine, in herbal teas, black tea, coffee, soft drinks and pharmaceuticals, is used widely to control sleepiness, but more research is needed on its use in sleep disorders. Ephedra, and its constituent ephedrine, are used in both stimulant and weight loss preparations, sometimes with caffeine; safety concerns have arisen with this practice. Yohimbe is another herb used in stimulant and body-building preparations which has safety concerns. Asian and Siberian ginseng have been traditionally used for fatigue, and have some supportive experimental evidence for this use. Herbal sedatives also have some evidence for efficacy; the observations that certain plant flavonoid compounds bind to benzodiazepine receptors adds interest to their use. Valerian and kava have received the most research attention; both have decreased sleep onset time and promoted deeper sleep in small studies, and kava also shows anxiolytic effects. German chamomile, lavender, hops, lemon balm and passionflower are reputed to be mild sedatives but need much more

Introduction

Healthy sleep can be defined as the quantity and quality of sleep needed to maintain optimal alertness during desired waking hours [1]. Studies have shown that difficulties with sleep and wakefulness are commonly found among 20–38% of the population in

various countries [2–5]. Insomnia, difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or early morning awakenings, is a common complaint with at least one symptom reported to occur a few nights of the week, or more often, among a 1998 representative sample of adults in the USA. Thirty-eight percent of adults in the USA in 1998 reported a level of daytime sleepiness that interfered with their daily activities for at least a few days a month; 18% reported difficulties at least a few days a week [6]. Ten to 15% of the US respondents reported using over-the-counter (OTC) medications or a dietary supplement to help them stay awake during the day. While 9% reported being diagnosed by a physician as having a sleep disorder, 20% reported taking a medicine prescribed by a physician to improve daytime alertness [7]. As we will demonstrate, the use of OTC and prescription wake- and sleep-promoting agents is now being augmented by use of herbal medicines for similar purposes. Healthcare providers have largely ignored this phenomenon in the past, but it is now becoming necessary for providers to educate themselves and their patients in the wise and unwise use of these agents. Providers involved in the care of persons with sleep disorders in particular must become sensitive to the potential impact of various herbal medicines on sleep problems. We will review the most widely available wake-promoting and sleep- promoting herbs in this paper: most of these have been commonly used in Europe in the past, but are new in the USA.

Normal sleep structure

The need for adequate quality and quantity of sleep is a biological drive similar to hunger and thirst that must be met in order for people to function appropriately in daily life [8]. Sleep is divided into two separate stages, non-rapid eye movement sleep (NREM Stages 1–4, 75–80% of total sleep) and rapid eye movement sleep (REM, 20–25% of total sleep) [9]. Stage 1 NREM sleep (2–5% of consolidated sleep), characterized by a low threshold for arousal, occurs at sleep onset and during stage transitions. Stage 2 NREM continues for 10–25 min after Stage 1, and has a much higher threshold for arousal. Deep sleep, Stages 3 and 4 of NREM sleep, comprises 13–23% of sleep time. During a REM period, rapid eye movements are observed, as well as an absence of muscle tone during REM sleep. The average period for alternating between NREM–REM is 90–110 min occurring in four to six episodes during sleep. When the sleep period is shortened or an inadequate amount of time is spent in Stages 3–4 NREM or REM sleep, the structure of sleep is disrupted. Difficulties with daytime performance or unwanted sleepiness during waketime are often manifestations of sleep stage disruption or insufficient sleep.

Sleep disorders

The majority of people seen in North American sleep disorder centers present with excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS). About 75% are eventually diagnosed with sleep apnea syndrome (SAS) and 20% with narcolepsy [10]. The obstructive form of SAS (OSA) is the most prevalent form and is characterized by repetitive episodes of upper airway obstruction during sleep that are manifested by snoring, or choking sounds. These episodes result in sleep fragmentation with frequent arousals from deeper to

Herbs and sleep 231

lighter sleep stages [11]. Narcolepsy is a chronic, neurological sleep disorder char- acterized by EDS with irresistible sleep attacks and the REM symptoms of cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations and sleep paralysis [12]. This disorder is treated symp- tomatically with central nervous system (CNS) stimulants to control EDS and anti- depressants to control the other REM symptoms. Anecdotally, patients with OSA and narcolepsy both report using OTC products, particularly caffeine, as adjunctive treatment to help control EDS.

Insomnia is a common symptom that is caused by a variety of health problems or life style situations, and is characterized by unrefreshing sleep as well as the inability to fall or remain asleep [13]. Behavioral interventions, such as stimulus control, sleep restriction and relaxation therapies, and pharmacological agents such as benzo- diazepines, are recommended for short-term management [13]. Due to the risk of physical dependence and the lack of clinical trial data for more than 35 days, the US Food and Drug Administration established guidelines that discourage the use of benzodiazepines and other hypnotic agents for longer than 4 weeks. Recurrence, safety concerns and the use of short-term efficacy strategies by health care practitioners may lead people to seek alternative OTC solutions for insomnia.

Complementary medicine and herbal agents

The use of complementary and alternative therapies not commonly taught in medical schools or available in hospitals has increased substantially worldwide, and in the USA during the current decade [14,15]. A survey in the USA indicated that 27% of the respondents used complementary therapies for fatigue and 26.4% for insomnia; about one-half of these respondents also saw a MD about their condition. The use of herbal remedies in the USA increased by 380% with 12.1% of the respondents reporting use in 1997 compared to 2.5% in 1990 [15]. One in five of the 1997 respondents reported this use was concurrent with prescription medications. Only 39% of the people using any complementary therapy shared this information with their conventional health care providers.

Use of herbal medicinals in the US market grew after the 1994 passage of the Dietary Supplements Health and Education Act. This act placed herbal medicines and other natural products under the new regulatory category of ‘‘dietary supplements’’. Dietary supplements are permitted to carry claims of useful effects on bodily structure or function on product packaging, but may not claim to prevent or treat disease. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not approve claims of this type prior to marketing of products, although manufacturers must submit the claims for approval before marketing begins, and must be prepared to validate the claims with scientific evidence. However, the proliferation of products has prevented the FDA from close inspection of most of them; thus many claims are being made for herbal and other products that are not well-supported by scientific literature. The herb industry is also permitted to engage in even less strictly regulated advertising in various news media, pamphlets made available in retail outlets, and, increasingly, on the Internet.

The variety of products that contain herbal medicines and other natural agents is also expanding. Herbal products, for the purposes of this paper, are defined as plant parts or extracts of plant parts, rather than single active compounds which can be extracted from plants and which are commonly sold as prescription or over-the-counter drugs (such as the cardiac drug digoxin, extracted from the foxglove, Digitalis lanata).

The traditional preparation of herbal medicines in Europe and most other countries has been herbal tea. Herbal teas are still widely used and available. Tinctures, or liquid alcoholic extracts which are taken in the form of drops, are also common. Capsules containing dried, powdered or freeze-dried herbs are common. Capsules may also contain dried alcoholic or water extracts of herbs. Herbs are now appearing in several other dosage forms, including chewable tablets, lozenges, lollipops, creams, and as a part of foods or vitamin–mineral preparations. The stability of active compounds in such dosage forms has not been studied. Another type of preparation which is growing in popularity is the essential oil or volatile oil, an extract of a fragrant herb species which contains fragrance-bearing compounds, such as terpenoids.

The standardized extract is another new type of herbal preparation. These extracts attempt to ensure comparable doses of active compounds in each dose of an herbal preparation; the first application of this concept in herbal studies was the use of standardized extracts in clinical trials. Plant species contain naturally varying amounts of different chemical compounds, including the compounds responsible for biological activities of herbal medicines. Batches of a single species grown in different areas, or in years with different climatic patterns, contain different amounts of such compounds. The standardized extract uses a procedure of extraction and concentration of varying batches of plant material to produce a product that has a guaranteed level of a particular active compound; more than one compound may be standardized in some preparations. In some medicinal plant species the identity of the active compound is not known; in such cases a compound unique to the plant species can be used as a ‘‘marker’’ compound. The use of standardized extracts diminishes the risk of con- tamination with toxic herbs because of mistaken identity, and eliminates herbs with suboptimal contents of active compounds. Manufacturing firms that use standardized extracts are also less likely to adulterate herbal preparations with prescription drugs or other such substances; addition of powerful prescription drugs to herbal extracts has been recorded several times for herbal preparations imported from China (where this practice has not always been considered unacceptable).

Wake-promoting preparations

Caffeine and caffeine-containing herbs

Caffeine, a mild stimulant, is a natural chemical found in the leaves, seeds or fruits of more than 60 plant species world-wide. Caffeine-containing plants primarily used as beverages include coffee, tea and a variety of other species such as kola, guarana and mate. Botanical and chemical data on these and other plants species discussed are shown in Table 1. The principal sources of caffeine are coffee and black or green tea [16]. Recently, beverages with guarana or mate as additives have begun to appear and are often labeled in a manner that makes them seem exotic. Other soft drink beverages containing significant amounts of caffeine have also been introduced. Some newer products are marketed as containing two or more times the amount of caffeine found in the older cola beverages; citrus-type beverages also contain more caffeine than most colas [17]. Other sources of caffeine include chocolate and cocoa foods (Theobroma cacao), and prescription and patent medications such as stimulants, pain relievers, diuretics, cold remedies and weight loss products [16]. Herbal products that feature caffeine-containing herbs include herbal teas (which include caffeine-containing species for both stimulant and taste effects), antioxidant preparations of green tea and weight loss formulas, which often combine caffeine with ephedrine-containing products, and a variety of laxative, diuretic and metabolic stimulant herbs.

Caffeine, a member of the methylxanthine drug class, putatively enhances alertness in humans by blocking the hypnogenic effects of adenosine, preventing this neuro- modulator from inhibiting areas of the brain that promote wakefulness. Additionally, caffeine increases excitatory neurotransmitter release. Since the synthesis, release and metabolism of neurotransmitters in the central nervous system are important in the regulation of the sleep–wake cycle, it is feasible to assume that caffeine intake during the day and before retiring will affect sleep and wakefulness [22].

Effects on sleep

Studies of caffeine administration have demonstrated that it affects the quantity and quality of sleep. In a survey of 140 college students, Pantelios et al. [23] found that subjects reporting a higher caffeine intake also reported taking longer to fall asleep and shorter sleep times. Similar impaired sleep was found among 48 low habitual caffeine use college students, half of whom blindly received caffeine 3–4 h before retiring [24]. In contrast, self-reported caffeine consumption spread out over waking hours has not been shown to be associated with sleeping difficulties in other samples [24, 25] suggesting that (1) people may adjust the timing of their caffeine intake to prevent

sleep problems and/or (2) the sensitivity to and tolerance of the sleep disruption effects of caffeine may vary between individuals.

The dose–response effects of caffeine have been demonstrated in the laboratory with middle-aged men when sleep parameters were objectively measured [26]. Total sleep time decreased and sleep latency increased. In light of the extent to which people report experiencing difficulties with their sleep, a careful history of caffeine intake needs to be taken that includes all possible sources of this compound. Among the elderly who have frequent sleep complaints and often poorer health, use of OTC caffeine-containing compounds needs especially to be considered.

Effects on sleepiness

The Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) is a polysomnographic procedure that measures how rapidly a person goes to sleep while comfortably lying down in a quiet, darkened room during four to five 20 min daytime nap opportunities (trials) spaced 2 h apart [27]. A mean MSLT score across the trials of <5 min is considered pathological, 5–10 min is considered a gray area and >10 min normal. The effects of caffeine on daytime sleepiness as measured by the MSLT were assessed among normal caffeine-consuming male subjects over 3–13 days of caffeine (dose=250 mg–400 mg once to three times a day) or placebo consumption while they maintained a regular sleep schedule [28–30]. The results of these studies were similar in that the mean MSLT score improved significantly compared to baseline following the initial day of caffeine administration, and fell somewhat on subsequent days, although the mean MSLT scores continued to significantly improve under the caffeine condition compared to baseline or placebo.

Additionally, several studies found improvement in MSLT scores during 3–49 h of forced sleep deprivation among healthy, low to moderate daily caffeine consumers under the caffeine condition as compared to placebo [31–33]. Significant increases in latencies were usually seen in a dose-related fashion with latencies often normalized to >10 min and responses lasting for 4–6 h.

Effects on sleep disorders

In our experience it is not unusual for people with sleep disorders that cause EDS to report using caffeine as a way to improve their level of alertness in addition to their prescribed therapy. However, data about the effectiveness of caffeine use among these individuals is notably lacking in the published literature. In the one published reference that could be found, Mitler et al. [34] presented interesting data showing that nar- coleptics reporting moderate or heavy caffeine use (125–500 mg/day) had lower scores on the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT) than non- or light users. (The MWT is a polygraphic test conducted in a similar manner to the MSLT, except that people are sitting comfortably in bed and instructed to try to stay awake instead of trying to go to sleep during the nap opportunities.) One possible explanation for this finding is that moderate and heavy users are significantly more sleepy than the none or light users and find some possible benefit from caffeine [34].

Ephedrine-containing herbs

Ephedra, or Ma Huang, is the plant source of the alkaloid ephedrine, one of the first drugs used in the treatment of narcolepsy [35]; it also contains pseudoephedrine. Since 1993 the US Food and Drug Administration has received over 800 reports of adverse

events related to dietary supplements containing ephedra alkaloids. About 40% of these related to serious clinical situations, the remainder to excessive stimulation. Ninety-two percent of the events related to products used for weight loss and energy enhancement, now the most common applications of this herb, which has been traditionally used in the treatment of asthma and congestion. Body building products and illicit street drugs comprised the remaining adverse events [36]. Of particular concern is the use of ephedra, or its alkaloids, together with caffeine-containing plants or caffeine, due to the possibility of interaction between ephedrine and caffeine. Adverse effects related to ephedrine alkaloids include tachycardia, arrhythmias, hyper- tension, chest pain, anxiety, nervousness, tremor, hyperactivity, insomnia, heart attack, stroke, psychosis, seizure and death [36]. Contraindications for ephedrine use include use of monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors, methyldopa, beta-blockers, or cardiac glycosides; presence of heart, thyroid or kidney disease; hypertension; depression or other psychiatric conditions, glaucoma; diabetes; enlarged prostate; and seizure disorders [36].

It is not clear how many adverse events relate to the pure alkaloids and how many to the use of the whole herb. The adverse event reports just discussed pertain almost exclusively to products containing the pure alkaloid, not the whole herb [36]. Doses of alkaloids may be lower in products containing the herb than in those containing isolated alkaloids, but they may still be sufficient to disturb sleep patterns in some individuals. Herbal weight loss preparations may also contain two other herbs, Indian sida and bitter orange, which contain ephedrine or related stimulant compounds (Table 1).

Yohimbe

Yohimbe bark is a reputed aphrodisiac used traditionally in African countries. It is the source of the drug yohimbine. A case report recounts the successful treatment of narcoleptic cataplexy with yohimbine in combination with paroxetine. Yohimbine was selected for cataplexy treatment because of its a-2 antagonist activity which leads to increases in synaptic norepinephrine; it is a powerful anticataplectic in dogs [37]. It also possesses MAO inhibition activity.

Yohimbe bark is found in herbal stimulants, sexual aids and body-building products. Yohimbine can have numerous side effects including nausea, vomiting, sweating, tachycardia and blood pressure increases; it should be avoided by individuals with kidney, heart or liver disease, ulcers, glaucoma or diabetes. Yohimbine has also been associated with a case of a lupus-like syndrome [38].

Ginseng

Ginseng, Panax ginseng, often called Asian or Korean ginseng to distinguish it from other plants called ginseng (e.g. Siberian ginseng and others), was traditionally used in Chinese medicine as a tonic or adaptogen, a substance which counteracts fatigue and non-specifically increases bodily resistance to various stressors. Ginseng is fre- quently used in the West as a performance enhancer or stimulant.

Ginseng contains compounds called ginsenosides, various triterpenoid saponin glycosides, as well as a wide variety of other compounds [39]. The literature on the

effects of these compounds is enormous and not always of good quality. Numerous effects of ginsenosides have been described, including increases in the ability of skeletal muscle to oxidize free fatty acids [40] and increased synthesis of acetylcholine and decreased brain serotonin [41].

Results of studies on the antifatigue activity of ginseng are conflicting; many studies suffer from poor design and inadequate numbers of subjects. Two small studies of exhaustive exercise showed no difference from placebo [42,43]. A number of studies, of both open and controlled design, were conducted by Forgo and colleagues using a standardized extract [44,45]. These studies indicated an improvement in aerobic cap- acity and reduction in blood lactate and heart rates during exercise. A double- blind crossover study in males of a ginseng–vitamin–mineral preparation found high tolerated exercise levels and oxygen uptake with ginseng administration [46].

Other studies on antifatigue effect did not examine athletic populations. A crossover study of ginseng in fatigued night nurses found a trend for improved mood, competence and performance with ginseng, although differences were not significant from placebo, perhaps because of low ginseng doses and a short study period [47]. Some participants reported less sleep and poor quality of sleep following ginseng use. Wiklund reported increased alertness, relaxation, appetite and quality of life from a ginseng– vitamin–mineral product in a controlled trial; no difference was reported from placebo on a sleep dysfunction scale used in the study [48]. A shorter study with the same product in elderly patients found no difference in quality of life; no sleep data were reported in this study [49].

A ‘‘syndrome’’ of supposed adverse effects of ginseng, which included hypertension, nervousness, insomnia and morning diarrhea was observed and widely publicized by Siegel [50]. These symptoms occurred after use of high doses of products whose ginseng content was not well specified. Some participants in the studies were drug addicts whose use of other substances was not controlled. These effects have not been observed in clinical trials. Ginseng is not included among the lists of banned stimulants for athletics [51]. However, there are more creditable reports of estrogenic effect, inhibition of clotting and interaction with the MAO inhibitor phenelzine [39].

Siberian ginseng

Siberian ginseng or eleuthero is a thorny shrub botanically related to Panax ginseng. It was first listed in the pharmacopoeia of the USSR in 1962; Soviet scientists conducted numerous studies on its performance-enhancing and adaptogenic effects during the 1960s and 1970s to determine its suitability as a less expensive substitute for Panax ginseng.

A series of compounds designated eleutherosides have been proposed as active compounds; these compounds have all, however, been isolated from other species under previously established chemical names [52].

Much of the work on the adaptogenic properties of Siberian ginseng focuses on its immunological effects, but there are animal studies and placebo-controlled human studies showing increases in physical endurance and work capacity [53].

Reports of adverse reactions to Siberian ginseng suffer from confusion with reports on Panax ginseng and from possible adulteration with the Chinese plant Periploca sepium. The latter species contains cardiac glycosides which may have been responsible for elevated serum digoxin levels in a heart patient taking Siberian ginseng [54]. A

baby with a profuse growth of hair on the head and pubic region was born to a mother taking a purported Siberian ginseng preparation [55]; both of these effects may be due to the adulterant [56].

Side effects noted in the human trials conducted in Russia include insomnia and disturbance of heart rhythms in elderly patients [57].

Herbal wake-promoting agents are not usually recommended to promote alertness by health care providers. However, some of the herbal wake-promoting agents, such as caffeine and ginseng, are legal and readily available, socially acceptable compounds that are probably used by some individuals to maintain alertness and counteract the effects of sleep loss. Other agents, such as ephedrine- or yohimbe-containing products, can have serious side effects and, even though they are legally available, individuals should be warned to avoid their use.

Persons with OSA or narcolepsy who are likely to suffer from EDS may be at particular risk for inappropriate use of herbal stimulants. Comorbidities such as diabetes and hypertension in which ephedrine use is contra-indicated are often found in individuals with severe OSA. Narcoleptics who perceive the control of their EDS to be inadequate with the traditionally prescribed stimulant medications may use herbal preparations along with prescribed medications to enhance alertness. People with both of these sleep disorders especially may need intensive counseling regarding herbal use.

Among some individuals, even caffeine and ginseng products should be avoided, notably use by the elderly who often experience disturbed night-time sleep, or are more likely to be on other medications that interact with herbal products as well as chronic insomniacs who are taking hypnotic medication. Additionally, individuals who take these products and ignore their biological need for sleep, or who suffer from sleep disorders, may live their lives in a chronically sleepy state, and may misperceive the extent of their sleepiness when compared to objective sleepiness measures. People with a chronic sleep debt who habitually use wake-promoting herbals as adjuncts to maintain alertness may experience a loss in effectiveness over time but be unable to comprehend the extent of their sleepiness. In addition to deficits in performance at work or school, these individuals may pose a public health hazard by contributing to the prevalence of workplace or automobile accidents due to misperceptions about their level of alertness. The higher rate of vehicular accidents among untreated OSA or narcolepsy patients is documented in current literature [58].

Herbal sedatives

Valerian

Valerian has been widely used in Europe since the 17th century and was formerly in the United States Pharmacopoeia. A series of non-glycosidated iridoids called valepotriates have been proposed as active constituents. Metabolites of these, baldrinal and homobaldrinal, show mutagenic activity in vitro but are lacking in typically used aqueous extracts and are rapidly detoxified in the liver; they probably do not pose clinical risks [59]. Valerenic acid is a sesquiterpene compound which may represent an active compound and is used in standardization.

Sedative properties of valerian are attributed to benzodiazepine-like activity and

effects on GABA. Research in Germany revealed that valerian extracts bind to benzo- diazepine receptors in vitro [60]. Later studies reported increased GABA concentrations in the synaptic cleft after valerian extract administration [61], but this was complicated by the presence of endogenous GABA in the aqueous extract used. A clinical example demonstrates valerian’s benzodiazepine-like activity: a patient who had been taking five to 40 times the recommended daily herb dose for years was hospitalized and received no valerian. He displayed symptoms resembling benzodiazepine withdrawal, and was then given benzodiazepines in a tapered dose, which resolved the symptoms [62].

Several human trials of valerian’s sedative effects have been performed, most with patients reporting sleep disorders. A German study reporting efficacy in sleep disorders enlisted 121 patients experiencing sleep difficulties for at least 4 weeks [63]. Depression and current use of sleep aids were exclusion criteria. The trial lasted 28 days; patients were administered either placebo or 600 mg valerian ethanol extract daily in a double- blind randomized trial. A physician-rated sleep scale, von Zerrsen mood scale, Gor- telmayer sleep questionnaire and Clinical Global Impressions scale were used to rate sleep quality. After 14 days there were no differences, but by 28 days the valerian group differed significantly from the placebo group in all scales. A small poly- somnographic study of elderly females reporting poor sleep (sleep latency over 30 min, more than three awakenings nightly, total sleep less than 5 h) included eight patients in an experimental and six patients in a control group [64]. Patients spent one adaptation night and two treatment nights in a sleep laboratory; valerian extract was given on the first treatment night and daily thereafter for a week until the second treatment night. Polysomnography showed increased slow-wave sleep in the experimental group on the second treatment night, as well as decreased Stage 1 sleep. There were no significant differences in sleep spindles on the three nights, but K complex density increased in the experimental group on the first and second treatment nights. No effects were seen in sleep latency or waking after sleep onset.

Decreases in sleep latency have been reported in other placebo-controlled trials, including those of Leathwood [65] and Balderer and Borbely [66]. In the latter trial the investigators compared one night of valerian and three nights of placebo in a sleep laboratory setting and a home study. Sleep latency, number of awakenings and EEG spectra did not differ in the laboratory study, but subjects in the home study reported decreased sleep latency and better sleep quality.

Residual sedative effects of valerian, a valerian/hops combination, flunitrazepam and placebo were studied in 80 patients by giving the four groups single doses of one of the four materials on the morning of the study [67]. On the afternoon of the study, and again on the following morning, tests of vigilance and reaction time were administered. The residual effects of the benzodiazepine at both times were significant, while those of the herbal remedies were not. Patients with temporary disorders of sleep onset and interruption were treated with a benzodiazepine or a hops-valerian preparation for 2 weeks in a randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; quality of life and sleep quality were equal in the two groups; only the benzodiazepine-treated group had withdrawal symptoms at the end of the treatment [68].

Reports of valerian toxicity are rare: a suicide attempt using 20 g of valerian (10 times the normal dosage) resulted in cramping and fatigue, and was resolved with activated charcoal. Use near conception and during pregnancy and lactation is not recommended due to possible mutagenic effects of valepotriates [59]. European clinical experience indicates that no interactions with alcohol or other drugs are to be expected,

and that residual morning sleepiness is uncommon [69]. Nevertheless, it seems wise to avoid use of valerian with alcohol and barbiturates, since it does prolong barbiturate sleeping time in animal studies. Patients wishing to use valerian for sleep disorders should be told that effects may not be seen until a few weeks of use, although this has not been observed in all studies.

German chamomile

German chamomile, Matricaria recutita, is more widely used than Roman chamomile, Anthemis nobilis. The two species are members of the daisy plant family and are used for similar purposes; there seem to be more reports of allergies associated with use of Roman chamomile. We will discuss the more common German chamomile in this review.

The sedative effects of chamomile are mild, and may be due to the flavonoid apigenin, which binds to benzodiazepine receptors [70]. It has an anxiolytic activity in mice, although the effective dose is approximately 10 times higher than that of diazepam. It has also shown anticonvulsant activity in mice [71], and CNS depressant activity in rats [72]. Clinical studies on the effects of chamomile on sleep are lacking. However, in a study which also demonstrated a weak hypertensive effect of chamomile,

12 hospitalized heart patients were given a strong chamomile tea. Ten of them immediately fell into a deep sleep lasting 90 min [73].

Allergenic activity has been reported for what appears to be German chamomile (scientific names were not always given in these reports). This activity seems largely to manifest itself as contact allergy or positive results on patch tests; individuals allergic to other members of the daisy plant family (Compositae or Asteraceae) may cross- react to chamomile [74]. Allergic reactions upon ingestion of chamomile are also possible, of course, although they do not appear to be a very significant problem.

Kava

Kava (or kava-kava) has long been used both ritualistically and socially by cultures in the South Pacific [75]. Recently, kava in various preparations has become popular in the United States and Europe where it is generally sold as a herbal supplement to treat anxiety and sleep disorders [75].

Research indicates that kava acts as a central nervous system depressant, and possesses muscle relaxant and analgesic activity in animals [75]. The kavapyrones or kavalactones (including kavain, methysticin, yangonin and dihydrokawain) have been shown to be responsible for these activities [76]. Recent studies have indicated that these compounds may influence GABA binding in certain areas of the brain [77].

Numerous studies have investigated the use of kava in the treatment of anxiety disorders. A purified kava preparation (standardized to 70% kavalactones) proved effective in some studies [78,79] with bioactivity comparable to benzodiazepines [80]. Another study demonstrated the effectiveness of the extract for the relief of psycho- autonomic symptoms (anxiety, restlessness, and sleep disturbances) associated with menopause [81]. The major chemical constituent of kava, kavain, is currently prescribed for anxiety in Europe [75].

The effectiveness of kava as a sleep aid has also been studied: in one study, kava

extract increased sleep spindle density with activity comparable to tranquilizers, and improved subjective parameters of sleep quality. Kava treatment also decreased sleep latency, duration of wake phase, and sleep stage 1; REM phase was unchanged with treatment [82]. Another study, however, showed that a chemical constituent of kava extracts, kavain, had no sleep inducing effects in healthy subjects. The authors of that study suggested, though, that kavain may improve sleep quality in subjects with anxiety-related sleep disturbances [83].

Due to the increasing use of kava preparations, possible adverse effects are a concern. Short-term clinical studies have shown that kava treatment (up to 600 mg) does not interfere with cognitive performance; psychometric tests show small but perceptible increases in cognitive function, evident in increased vigilance and enhanced memory [84–86]. Safety-related performance studies indicate that kava extract (3×100 mg/day) did not affect driving ability or work safety [87] and did not potentiate the effects of alcohol [88] or benzodiazepine drugs [89]. A report of a possible interaction between a kava product and alprazolam, a benzodiazepine, does not rule out the possibility that the adverse effects were associated solely with the benzodiazepine [90, 91]. Studies that demonstrate no cognitive functional impairment from kava are supported by evidence that EEG profiles of subjects treated with kava extract (up to 600 mg) show a typical anxiolytic pattern without the sedative-hypnotic effects as- sociated with benzodiazepines [92].

Long-term studies are extremely important as the treatment of anxiety disorders often requires extended treatment. Numerous clinical studies using a purified kava extract (standardized to 70% kavalactones) in dosages of 3×100 mg/day for up to 8 weeks reported no adverse reactions to the extract [78–81]. In one 25 week study, the same kava preparation was very well tolerated [79,83]. However, some reports describe a severe but reversible dermopathy and yellowish skin discoloration among members of Pacific island and Australian aborigine cultures with prolonged use of kava in dosages 10–100 times those used clinically [93]. The yellow color of the skin in these cases is not due to hepatic damage but to a pigment deposited in skin cells that degrades with time when kava intake ceases. In addition, isolated cases report cutaneous allergic reactions resulting from use of the herb [94].

Lavender

In folklore, linen bags were filled with lavender flowers and placed under the pillow to prevent problems in falling asleep. There is suggestive evidence that lavender essential oil may be helpful in management of certain sleep disorders; the German Commission E monographs [69] include ‘‘states of unrest and difficulty falling asleep’’ under indications for internal use of lavender. Lavender oil therapy is typically given by breathing the volatilized oil, referred to as ‘‘aromatherapy’’.

The main chemical constituents of lavender are camphor, linalyl acetate, linalool, beta-ocimene, and eucalyptol. The herb also contains up to 12% tannins. Phar- macological studies have only reported on lavender oil, the extract which contains most of these compounds.

Experimental evidence indicates that lavender essential oil has a depressive effect on the central nervous system. In various animal studies, lavender demonstrated strong CNS depressant activity with sedative, anticonvulsive, anxiolytic, motor inhibitory and spasmolytic effects [95]. Caffeine-induced hyperactivity in mice was reduced to nearly

normal locomotor activity only by inhalation of lavender (injection was ineffective) [96]. In a multiple crossover study of 23 female subjects suffering from sleep disorders, lavender demonstrated CNS-depressant activity via EEG recordings [97]. The oil has also demonstrated effectiveness in improving sleep quality via inhalation: patients experienced a reduction in restlessness during sleep [98]. In 40 adults given 3 min of lavender aromatherapy, subjects were more relaxed, their moods were less depressed (POMS), and they performed math computations faster and more accurately following

aromatherapy [99].

Although no toxicity has been reported for lavender, it does potentiate the sleep- inducing activity of some other agents, such as alcohol, chloral hydrate, and Evipan [95].

Hops, lemon balm and passionflower

Little clinical study has been done on these minor herbal sedatives. Botanical data and possible active compounds in these herbs are listed in Table 1. Animal studies have indicated potential sedative effects for all three [75]. One of the human studies, a double-blind crossover study of 27 subjects with sleep difficulties taking hops, lemon balm and valerian, showed no sleep enhancement with hops or lemon balm, while 89% of subjects reported improved sleep with valerian [100].

Reports of toxicity of the minor sedative herbs are rare. Animal studies show barbiturate potentiation effects, and a study in a related species of passionflower not used in herbal medicine revealed hepatobiliary and pancreatic toxicity [101]. As with all other herbal preparations, these herbs should not be taken during pregnancy and lactation.

Discussion

In considering both the pharmacology of herbal stimulants and sedatives, and their patterns of use in the current market, several summary points are evident. Although much work has been done on these substances (see Table 3), much remains to be done to understand their safety and efficacy. Exploration of herb–drug interaction is needed, and may be especially relevant in elderly patients who take numerous prescription drugs, and who frequently complain of sleep problems. Continued research is also needed on such basic questions as the identity of active compounds and their stability in different preparations. The prevalence of adulteration and contamination in herbs should be examined, especially those imported from areas where their manufacture is not closely regulated; the increasing use of standardized preparations should, however, help alleviate such problems. The activity of herbal sedatives in sleep initiation versus sleep maintenance should be explored. The relative lack of side effects and morning-after effects of herbal sedatives may make them useful adjuncts to the conventional behavioral treatment of insomnia; research on this possibility is warranted. Because of widening popular use of herbs, non-judgmental questions on their use must become standard in medical histories, especially with patients with sleep problems and those from cultures in which herb use is common.

Individual herbal substances also deserve certain comments. The use of herbal stimulants, and especially of caffeine, the most widely used plant-derived stimulant, needs to be carefully examined in health care settings. control the symptoms of a more serious sleep disorder. We noted an appalling lack of research on the patterns of use, and the efficacy and safety of caffeine in management of chronic sleep disorders. This is especially distressing in view of the frequency of clinical encounters with patients who use caffeine to manage EDS, and the recognized potential for development of caffeine tolerance. Caffeine and Panax ginseng, however, are both relatively safe and mild preparations in comparison with other conventional and herbal stimulants, and research should examine whether their use may be war- ranted as adjuncts to control residual sleepiness among patients with sleep disorders who are already in conventional treatment. There are safety concerns with some herbal stimulants, especially ephedra or ephedrine, which are used with caffeine in weight loss preparations. Yohimbe is another herbal stimulant with some safety concerns.

Although the herbal sedatives all need much more research, some interesting preliminary data have been noted. Valerian, widely used in Europe, has been shown to decrease sleep latency and, in a small study, to increase slow-wave sleep and decrease Stage 1 sleep. Its favorable side effect profile indicates that it may be worth using in experimental trials in patients who have difficulty using conventional sedatives. Kava has also shown an ability to decrease sleep latency and Stage 1 sleep, and has demonstrated anxiolytic properties. It has a favorable side effect profile when used in reasonable doses, and might be useful in experiential trials, especially for persons with anxiety-related insomnia and difficulties with sleep onset. Effects of the other herbal sedatives discussed all need much more experimental validation.

As scientific understanding of herbal medicines advances, our ability to integrate useful findings on herbal stimulants and sedatives into clinical protocols will increase. The time has already arrived, however, for health professionals to become conversant with the variety of herbal substances from different cultures that have now entered the world market, and to realize the important role they play today in the self- management of sleep problems.

Practice Points

The medication history taken by a health care professional needs to include non- judgmental questions about the use of herbal wake-promoting and sleep aid preparations.

Special attention should be paid to the undisclosed use of these preparations among people with chronic sleep or problem sleepiness complaints not adequately addressed with conventional treatment.

Standardized herbal products are likely to be the most reliable and predictable dosage forms.

Because of inadequate knowledge of possible adverse effects, herbal medicines should be used cautiously, especially when OTC or prescription medicines are used concomitantly.

People who chronically overlook their biologic need for sleep may be at high risk for the use of herbal wake/sleep supplements.

Research Points

Data regarding the incidence of use of herbals by people with sleep disorders need to be systematically collected.

Herbal sedative and anxiolytic preparations would profit from large-sample

double-blind, placebo-controlled trials with normals to fully characterize their properties.

Evidence to support or refute the efficacy of wake- or sleep-promoting herbal medicinals for people with sleep disorders should be gathered.

The adverse reactions to, and interactions with, other compounds need to be more systematically studied for all of the wake- and sleep-promoting herbal agents.
